findings.quote: A seed is made of living cells, even when it looks inactive.
findings.problem: This general rule fails at a known exception. A seed can die: an old stored seed loses viability, and a boiled or roasted seed is dead. Its cells are no longer living, so it will never sprout. The same absolute sits in Core Concept: 'A dry seed does not grow, move, or react for a long time. It is still alive.' The lesson then contradicts itself, because Example #5 step 3 gives a sprouting test ('If it sprouts and grows, it was alive'), which would be pointless if every seed were alive. A student who learns 'a dry seed is always alive' will call a dead or cooked seed living, and learns to decide by category instead of by evidence, which is the lesson's own goal.
findings.source: OpenStax Biology 2e, 32.2 Pollination and Fertilization, Germination ('Many mature seeds enter a period of inactivity ... known as dormancy'; many, not all); seed viability declines in storage (standard seed-testing practice); content-checklist B01; reader-rules.md, Added after the Sol audit
